LD2450 · SAVED USB CAPTURE · 6 OCTOBER 2026

A quiet office, seen through two radar receivers

The data is transport-clean and strongly repeatable. This is a useful static baseline, with rich complex samples, but it is not yet a calibrated map of objects or distances.

The user reports that the radar faced approximately toward their keyboard in an unattended office. This report analyzes the existing 30-second recording only; it does not access the device.

Clean transport, measurable analog variation

Every accepted lane file matches its saved SHA-256. Every reconstructed record independently passes header, receiver/chirp sequence, trailer and radar checksum checks. The original receiver also validated all message and reconstructed-record CRCs. The capture ends with an incomplete frame, which is excluded. This establishes intact transport, not a noiseless radar receiver.

The residual includes electronic noise, repeatable ripple, drift and any small real scene changes. These ratios are repeatability measurements, not calibrated target SNR. Large I/Q offsets and static reflections dominate the raw values. No samples reach the exported signed-16-bit limits; the physical ADC range is not established.

The scene is not mathematically constant: the dominant coefficient amplitude falls by about 4.0% on RX1 and 3.2% on RX2, while the relative phase drifts about 0.45 degrees (first versus last ten frames). Slow settling or temperature drift are possible explanations, but no temperature or independent motion reference was recorded.

How far, and how detailed?

Hi-Link specifies the stock LD2450 for up to 6 m, approximately ±60° in azimuth, and 250 MHz sweep bandwidth. Those are module specifications, not a demonstrated range for this custom firmware or this office recording. Manufacturer manual, V1.02, section 8.

At 250 MHz, the ideal FMCW two-target range-resolution scale is c/(2B) ≈ 0.60 m when using the full linear sweep. Windowing and partial-sweep acquisition can worsen separation. Estimating one isolated target's position can be more precise than separating two nearby targets. The 512 samples are not 512 independently resolved objects, and they do not establish a centimetre-spaced range grid. Our actual sample rate, sweep slope and sample-to-sweep alignment still need confirmation.

Complex I/Q retains amplitude and phase; the two receivers provide information for direction estimation. After calibration we can investigate distance, radial motion, hand/gesture changes and fine phase changes. Breathing or tiny vibration sensing is a hypothesis to test with controlled displacement, not a capability demonstrated by this recording. A static reflection can reveal an object, but cannot by itself identify an immobile person.

A small timing issue to keep separate from signal noise

Median adjacent-chirp spacing is 1.200 ms, and frame IDs imply a radar frame period of 88.987 ms (11.24 Hz). Only selected complete frames were exported. Eight of 20,034 interval entries are anomalous: two chirp events, on both receivers, have a roughly 0.199 ms interval followed by 2.200 ms. This looks like timestamp bookkeeping near a 1 ms timer boundary, but the cause has not been proven. Record identities and checksums remain intact. Doppler plots use nominal spacing and are exploratory. Original timestamps are preserved.

Next measurements that would answer the remaining questions

  1. Keep the radar fixed; place one strong reflector at measured distances, for example 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 m, with an empty-scene reference. Determine the right sweep segment and calibrate the frequency-to-distance slope.
  2. Move the same reflector toward and away from the board. Identify Doppler sign, static-clutter removal behavior and usable motion sensitivity.
  3. At fixed range, move the reflector left, center and right. Calibrate receiver phase offset and confirm the phase-to-angle relationship.
  4. Compare quiet and powered/active desk equipment states to investigate the narrow ±220-bin feature before calling it a physical target.

Reproduce with python tools/analyze_usb_frames.py. Exact input hashes are in source_manifest.json; numerical results and limitations are in analysis.json. PNG and SVG charts are retained beside this self-contained report.
